judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 176. It lets people pick up several months of birth control at a time. The rule applies to a health plan that already covers contraceptive drugs. It does not make any plan start covering them. Where a plan does cover them, it must let the member collect a three-month supply the first time, and a six-month supply each time after that. That holds even if the member was on a different plan the first time. Only one six-month supply may be collected in any six-month period. A member may still ask for less, and a prescriber may still write less where that is the right clinical choice. The act says plainly that it does not require any plan to cover medicine that could end a pregnancy. The Oklahoma House passed it 65-25. It became law without the Governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1443. It tells health plans to take account of how sick a patient is when they pay for anesthesia. Anesthesia is the medicine that puts a patient to sleep or blocks pain for an operation. When a plan decides whether that care was needed and what to pay for it, the act makes it weigh two things. The first is the patient's physical condition, graded on a standard scale by the treating doctor. The second is how complex and how urgent the care was, again as the treating doctor judges it. The act then fixes what the sickest patients are worth in payment terms. A patient with severe disease adds one base unit, one whose disease is a constant threat to life adds two, and one not expected to survive without the operation adds three. Plans that cover Medicaid members under a separate state act are outside this rule. The Oklahoma House passed it 68-17. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to override the Governor's veto of Senate Bill 631. It adds crimes to the list where most of the sentence must be served before parole. Oklahoma keeps a list of serious crimes for which a person must serve at least eighty-five percent of the sentence before becoming eligible for parole. The act adds firing a gun at or into a home, or into a building used for public or business purposes. It also extends the whole list to an attempt at any of those crimes, and to conspiring or soliciting someone to commit one. The rest of the act tidies the list: it renames child pornography as child sexual abuse material, corrects two wrong section numbers, and drops one cross-reference from the rape entry. The Oklahoma House voted 68-17 to override the veto. The Senate had already done the same, so the bill became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1833. It moves to stop food aid being spent on sweets and fizzy drinks. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, is federal food aid, so the state cannot narrow it on its own. The act tells the Department of Human Services to ask the federal government for a waiver, and to bar candy and soft drinks once that waiver is granted. The Director may seek to exclude other food the Director judges to have no nutritional value. The waiver request must argue public health, the purpose of the program in law, and savings to taxpayers. It must show that shop tills can enforce the rule, set out how recipients will be told about healthier options, and track what the change does to spending and to health. If the waiver comes through, the department has six months to bring the restriction in, and it reports to the Governor and legislative leaders each year. The Oklahoma House passed it 62-17. The Governor signed it.
